turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mrs Pillay, come through, both of you. Your daughter phoned about falls, so I want your version first. What happened?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't fall, Doctor. I slid down, twice, and I'm scared it's a stroke like the neighbour. Am I going to hospital?
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ma, you fell. Tuesday, hard, on the bathroom tiles, and Thursday getting out of bed you hit the cupboard. There was a bruise on the left hip.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ag, that mark is old. I slid, my legs went soft, it was not a fall. I can't tell you which day, it blurs. Is sliding counted as a fall?
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll come back to the wording. When you stand, do you feel dizzy?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. The room goes a bit swimmy, only on standing, not when I sit with tea. Will it happen at church?
[SEG0007] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three weeks now, since the church bazaar. She holds the wall the whole way to the kitchen.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only since Saturday, two days, maybe three. I was fine at the bazaar, I had a scone.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So you're apart on the timing, a couple of days versus a few weeks. Any chest pain with the dizzy spells?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Dis-Chem in Plumstead was hectic, the queue by the vitamins, and load shedding killed the card machine. I nearly left with nothing.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): The tablets can wait. Pain or pressure in the chest when you stand — yes or no?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. My heart thumps afterwards, or maybe I'm just worked up. Am I dying?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not dying in this room. The pressure tablets can drop you on standing, and the sleeping tablet can leave you unsteady.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): An inner-ear problem or a heart-rhythm glitch, I won't cross those off yet. I'm not calling it a stroke. The leading picture, for me, is a postural drop.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I stop all the tablets? I don't have sugar tablets, those were my husband's, and he's late. What do I take instead?
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Dad died last year, she muddles that. Hers are the water tablet, the white pressure one, Coversyl, and the blue sleeping tablet.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Start with the water tablet. Is that Ridaq, hydrochlorothiazide, and what dose?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the little water tablet, twenty-five milligrams, every morning with tea. It makes me wee all morning. If it stops, will my legs balloon?
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): They might puff a bit, we'll watch. The white one — name and strength?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Amlodipine, I think five milligrams. Unless five is the other tablet. Is five dangerous for someone my age?
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cupboard box says amlodipine ten milligrams, one in the morning. I've checked it.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then the amlodipine stays as it is until I see that box. Five and ten can't both be right. And Coversyl?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Coversyl four milligrams every morning, for the pressure. I've had the pressure since about sixty, and I'm seventy-eight. Is four too much?
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four is ordinary, it stays. Tell me about the sleeping tablet.

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one, Imovane. Not half — the whole seven point five — at bedtime, most nights, and sometimes another at two if I wake. Is that poison, and will I ever sleep without it?
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Not most nights. About four nights a week. And she's foggy those mornings, she even misses her tea.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Foggy mornings can be the Imovane, but I'm not stopping it today. Any tablet besides those?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): A small yellow one from the hospital clinic. I can't remember the name, bones or cholesterol, I don't know which. Must I throw it away?
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't throw it. Bring the bottle. Any drug allergies?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. I can take anything. Are you going to give me penicillin? I saw a poster.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The hospital said penicillin. She got a rash when she was younger and they told her to avoid it. She just won't keep it in her head.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): It was the heat, not a rash. I am not allergic. Can I still do communion on Sunday, all the standing?
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Penicillin stays noted as disputed, not confirmed. Sister checked the pressures before you came in.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lying was one hundred and forty-six over eighty-four, pulse seventy-six. Standing after a minute, one hundred and twelve over seventy, pulse ninety-four. That's a proper drop. It fits the postural picture.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Is one twelve too low? Will I faint at Checkers? Should I drink more water, and how much?

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): One hundred and twelve can be adequate; it's the drop that matters. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur, and the chest is clear. I don't see a fresh bruise on the hip. Did you black out either time?
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Left hip, it was purple on Thursday. She's shy to show you. It looks yellow now.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I never blacked out, I knew where I was, just ashamed. The tiles are slippery, and my cousin in Durban broke her wrist that way. Must I sell the house?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): You don't need to sell the house. Are you short of breath walking or on standing?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really, no. I am very tired by lunchtime, though. Is that the tablets, and will one change fix it?

[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She naps all afternoon. She doesn't drink and she doesn't smoke. She stays with me in Plumstead, and I'm at work till four so she's alone. She won't admit that worries her.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations? And family illness, apart from the neighbour stories?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Gallbladder out, fifteen years back, at Groote Schuur, nothing else. My mother had sugar, diabetes. How would I know if I had it? I don't want it.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thirst and weight loss would be the clues, and I'm not diagnosing diabetes off your mother. Today I'm changing one tablet only.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the water tablet, Ridaq, the hydrochlorothiazide twenty-five milligrams, from today. It can drop the pressure when you stand. Coversyl stays, amlodipine waits for the box, and no second Imovane at two in the morning.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): If the water tablet stops, will the pressure shoot up? How high is dangerous? Should I buy my own machine?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't know until we recheck. I'd like kidney function and a sodium today, and an ECG after this. I'm not deciding it's the heart, and I still won't exclude a rhythm problem. If the dizziness hasn't settled in two weeks, we might do a Holter, a day-long monitor.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Please write it down, she won't remember. And the yellow tablet, what do we do with that?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring every box next visit, yellow one included. I can't name a tablet from small and yellow. Follow up here in two weeks, with the boxes.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks feels long. If I slide tonight, do I phone an ambulance? Is that a stroke? I didn't sleep, worrying.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you black out, can't get up, or there's one-sided weakness or slurred speech, that's an ambulance. If you just slide and you're yourself, sit and phone your daughter. Get up in stages — sit, count to twenty, then stand. No rushing to the loo in the dark.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Count to twenty, I'll try. And church, communion, the standing?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Church is fine. Sit at the end of the pew, and skip a hymn if you go swimmy. Any headache, fever, or burning when you wee?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No headache, no fever. Waterworks are fine apart from weeing a lot from that water tablet. Must we replace all the tiles? I'm so scared of a broken wrist.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): A mat, Ma, not a new floor. Doctor, please don't write only slides. There were two falls. She always minimises.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): They were slides. I didn't fall. I don't want falls on a letter, people will think I can't cope. Will the letter go to my medical aid?

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll record both. You describe two slides, conscious the whole time. Your daughter describes two falls and a hip bruise I can't confirm today. The tests don't settle that argument.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): The ECG doesn't hurt. Bloods today, I see them in a day or two, and tea after the needle so the sodium is true. See you in two weeks.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Tea after, alright. I'm still nervous, but I'll count to twenty. Thank you, Doctor. Is two weeks definitely enough?
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll bring every box. Come on, Ma, the sister is waiting for the tracing.
